overview: Wu was a lower-Yangtze kingdom that became a major rival of Chu, Yue and the northern states during the late Spring and Autumn period. This map uses an approximate 1500 to 500 BCE span and one broad outline: neither establishes its founding or changing frontiers. Its final royal generation and conquest in 473 BCE occurred after the map cutoff and are included here as later history.

periods.title: Regional communities before the best-documented kings
periods.summary: Rice and millet remains illuminate regional farming centuries before Wu’s final struggles. These dates describe archaeological context, not an established founding year.

periods.title: Inscribed kings and growing power
periods.summary: The surviving bronze catalogue includes Shoumeng and subsequent rulers, followed by the reign of Guang, better known as Helu.

periods.title: Later history: Fuchai and conquest
periods.summary: After the imported map endpoint, Fuchai challenged other states before Yue conquered Wu in 473 BCE.

items.text: Wu’s named royal sequence is much firmer in the sixth century BCE than in the distant starting date printed on this map. Inscribed weapons record rulers, sons and brothers. The scholarly catalogue arranges objects under Shoumeng, Zhufan, Yuji and later kings, giving historians evidence beyond stories told long afterward.

Under Helu, Wu defeated its rival Chu in 506 BCE. His son Fuchai then defeated Yue, forcing its ruler Goujian to seek peace. Wu’s ambitions also reached north toward Jin. Several powerful states competed for regional supremacy.

Fuchai became king in 495 BCE and defeated Goujian the next year. In 482 BCE he met the ruler of Jin at Huangchi. Those dated episodes belong to the kingdom’s final decades, which this particular map layer does not reach.

In 486 BCE Fuchai ordered the Han Gou canal between the areas of Yangzhou and Huaian as part of his northern ambitions. This early waterway later became part of the much larger Grand Canal system. The enormous canal familiar from later Chinese history grew through many subsequent dynasties; Wu did not build the whole thing.

At Jingshuidun in southern Anhui, researchers found rice and foxtail millet in layers dating approximately to the eighth and seventh centuries BCE. This gives a local view of farming in the broader lower-Yangtze region. It does not prove that every settlement under Wu ate the same meals.

The Jingshuidun study counted 44 rice remains and 92 foxtail millet remains in its late Western Zhou to early Spring and Autumn samples. Seeds and microscopic plant traces can reveal work that royal inscriptions barely mention: growing and handling food. Those counts describe the excavated samples, not the proportions on a family’s dinner plate.

A dugout canoe found in Yancheng’s inner watercourse in 1965 was made from nanmu timber and measured 7.45 metres long. Its survival offers a tangible glimpse of boatbuilding in the region of Wu. A boat carved from one tree still demanded considerable knowledge of wood and a good deal of careful work.

Ancient wood needs care even after it reaches a museum. The Yancheng canoe suffered cracking, pieces coming apart and shrinkage. In 2020 Wujin Museum’s conservation planning included a three-dimensional model and a detailed condition assessment before specialists discussed how to protect it. Finding an object is only the beginning of keeping it safe.

At Mudu near Suzhou, archaeologists identified substantial walls, waterways, workshops and burial remains. A water gate near Lake Tai and traces of a stone road show that movement by water and movement on land were both part of the settlement. The precise identification of Wu’s capital remains debated.

Pottery and stone tools help fill out that urban picture. Investigations around Mudu recovered patterned pottery along with stone knives, axes and chisels. They bring craft work and useful everyday equipment into a story otherwise dominated by royal bronzes and campaigns.

A bronze wine vessel records a marriage connection between Cai and Wu in 518 BCE. The Lord of Cai commissioned it for Da Meng Ji as a bridal vessel. Here a named woman appears in evidence of diplomacy between ruling families. This royal alliance tells us about elite marriage, rather than everyone’s family arrangements.

The vessel came from the Lord of Cai’s tomb at Shouxian, excavated in 1955. Its 486 bronzes included instruments, weapons and containers for food, wine and water. Their varied forms connect Cai with both the Central Plains and Chu, while inscriptions document its relationships with Wu. The tomb belonged to Cai, Wu’s neighbour and marriage partner.

A bronze sword bearing Fuchai’s name combines a ridged blade with patterned decoration and a beast-mask guard inlaid with turquoise. Weapons could display fine craft as well as military power. The tiny coloured inlays would have required skills quite different from shaping and sharpening the blade.

Fuchai’s bronze jian belongs to a type of large water container that could hold water for looking at one’s reflection or ice for cooling food. Large examples also served in ceremony or display. Imagine checking your face in a bowl! This is a possible vessel function, not Fuchai’s documented routine.

That royal basin has animal-head handles, intricate curling decoration and a tiger crouching on its rim with its head peeking out. Inside, a thirteen-character inscription records Fuchai’s commission. Even a practical vessel could become an elaborate statement of royal ownership.

An excavated spear preserves the words 吳王夫差, “King Fuchai of Wu.” These are modern Chinese character forms transcribing the beginning of the ancient inscription, not a facsimile of its decorative lettering. The scholarly corpus prints the same opening across several published readings. It is a genuine early-fifth-century royal witness, later than this map’s 500 BCE endpoint.

The Hubei Provincial Museum dates this spear to the late Spring and Autumn period and records its excavation from Mashan tomb 5 at Jiangling in 1983. Its surviving bronze head is 29.5 centimetres long. The place where a weapon was buried is not automatically the place where its named ruler lived.

ending.text: Yue conquered Wu in 473 BCE, ending Fuchai’s monarchy. That event falls after the imported map’s 500 BCE cutoff. The surviving objects preserve evidence of royal power, craft and regional life beyond stories of its kings.
